The thing that gets lost in these threads is that "self-driving" was never one problem with one finish line. Waymo running driverless in a handful of sunbelt cities with heavy mapping, remote assistance, and conservative operating domains is a real and impressive achievement. It's also not remotely what was being sold in 2016, when we were told you'd be able to summon your car across the country and rent it out as a robotaxi while you slept. Both camps keep talking past each other because one is pointing at Phoenix and the other is pointing at a snowy two-lane road in Vermont at night.

The long tail is the whole game, and it's brutal. Getting to 99% is an engineering problem; getting from 99.99% to whatever humans actually achieve (roughly one fatality per 100 million miles in the US) is closer to a research problem, and nobody has a credible timeline for it. Every time a company announces a breakthrough, it turns out to be a better handle on the cases they'd already seen, not a general solution to the ones they haven't. Construction zones with a guy waving a hand-drawn sign, a ball rolling into the street, a cop overriding a signal: these aren't edge cases you patch, they're the actual texture of driving.

I don't think it's vaporware, and I'd bet we get broad geofenced robotaxi coverage in most major metros within a decade. But "your personal car drives itself anywhere, no wheel required" keeps slipping five years out, every year, and I've stopped treating any date attached to it as information. The most useful heuristic I've found: discount any timeline from someone whose stock price depends on it.

I remember sitting in a talk around 2016 where someone confidently said their kid would never need a driver's license. That kid is driving now. The thing that gets me isn't that the timelines slipped, since everything slips, it's that the people making the predictions had the data to know better and said it anyway because it was good for fundraising and stock price.

To be fair, Waymo works. I've ridden in one a bunch of times in Phoenix and it's honestly boring in the best way. But it took 15+ years, enormous amounts of money, detailed mapping, remote assistance, and careful selection of cities with good weather and wide roads. That's a real achievement, but it's not "your car drives you anywhere while you sleep," which is what was being sold to the public. The last few percent of edge cases turned out to be most of the problem, which anyone who's shipped software could have told you.

What I'd actually like to see is people being honest that this is going to look like a slow city-by-city rollout over decades, not a switch that flips. Snow, rural roads, construction zones with a guy waving a hand-written sign, those are still hard. I'll believe the "next year" claims when I can take one from my house in Michigan to my parents' place in January.

I've been fully remote since March 2020, and the thing nobody warned me about is that the hard part isn't productivity, it's visibility. My output went up. I ship more, I'm interrupted less, and my code reviews are more thorough because I'm not context-switching every twenty minutes for someone's "quick question." But when promo season came around, the people who got the nod were disproportionately the ones who'd gone back to the office three days a week. Not because they did more, but because they were the ones the director remembered talking to. Remote work doesn't just change how you work, it changes how you have to advertise your work, and a lot of engineers (myself included) were slow to figure that out.

That said, I think the "return to office" push at a lot of companies is less about collaboration and more about managers who never learned to manage outcomes instead of presence. If you can only tell someone is working by seeing them at a desk, that's a skill gap, not a remote work problem. The teams I've seen thrive remotely all have one thing in common: they write things down. Decisions live in docs, not in hallway conversations that half the team missed. Async by default, sync when it actually matters.

The honest answer is it's a tradeoff that depends heavily on career stage. Senior folks with established networks and clear scope do great remote. Juniors often struggle, because so much of learning the job is osmosis: overhearing how someone debugs a prod issue, or getting pulled into a whiteboard session you didn't know you needed. I don't think the answer is forcing everyone back, but companies that went fully remote without deliberately replacing that mentorship layer are going to feel it in five years when their mid-level bench is thin.

I had this happen last year and it still bugs me. I was writing a pretty boring ring buffer in C, nothing special, and Copilot autocompleted about 30 lines. The variable names were oddly specific, and there was a comment with a typo in it that I definitely didn't write. I grepped GitHub for the typo and found it in a GPL'd embedded project. It was verbatim, comment and all. If I hadn't been paying attention, that would have gone straight into a proprietary codebase at work.

The usual reply is "it's just learning patterns, like a human reading code." Sure, for most suggestions that's probably true. But a human who memorized 30 lines including someone's typo and pasted them into a commit would be in trouble, and "I read it once" isn't a defense anyone would accept. The duplicate detection filter exists now, which is basically GitHub admitting the problem is real. In my experience it catches the obvious stuff and misses anything with the identifiers slightly changed.

What I actually want is provenance. Tell me "this suggestion closely matches X, licensed under Y" and let me decide. Code search already does something like this, so it's clearly technically doable. Until that's the default, our team policy is that Copilot output gets treated like a snippet from a random forum post: fine for ideas, rewrite it before it ships.

**Title: I quit my 9-to-5 last Friday to run my app full time. Terrified and thrilled.**

After three years of building nights and weekends, I finally pulled the trigger. My app (a scheduling tool for small fitness studios) crossed $6k MRR last month, which covers my bills with a little left over. Not exactly retirement money, but enough to bet on myself.

The hardest part wasn't the math. It was walking away from a stable salary, health insurance, and a team I genuinely liked. My manager was supportive, which somehow made it harder.

Here's what I did to prepare:
- Saved 9 months of expenses
- Waited until revenue was consistent for 6+ months
- Lined up my own health coverage before giving notice

Now I have 40 extra hours a week and zero excuses.

For those who've made the jump: what do you wish you'd known in your first 90 days?

**Title: My smart speaker recorded a private conversation and I only found out by checking the activity log**

So last week I was digging through my voice assistant's app settings (long overdue, I know) and decided to look at the stored voice history. I expected a list of "what's the weather" and "set a timer for 10 minutes." What I actually found was a 40-second clip of my partner and me arguing about finances in the kitchen. Nobody said the wake word. The log labeled it "audio not intended for device."

So it knew it wasn't meant for it, kept it anyway, and uploaded it to the cloud.

I've since deleted my history and turned on auto-delete, but it got me thinking: how often does this happen? Who has access to these clips before they're "deleted"? Are they used for training?

Yes, you can, especially for simpler projects. Here are your main options:

**No-code platforms:** Tools like Bubble, Adalo, Glide, FlutterFlow, and Softr let you build apps with drag-and-drop interfaces. They work well for things like booking systems, directories, internal tools, and MVPs.

**AI app builders:** Tools like Lovable, Bolt, and Replit can generate working apps from plain-English descriptions. You describe what you want and refine it through conversation.

**Spreadsheet-based tools:** Glide and AppSheet can turn a Google Sheet into a functional app in an afternoon.

**The caveats:** You'll eventually hit limits with complex logic, performance, or customization. Costs can grow as you scale, and you're tied to the platform. Debugging AI-generated code is hard if you don't understand it.

**My advice:** Start with no-code to validate your idea quickly. If it gains traction, either learn some basics or bring in a developer. Learning a little logic (variables, conditions, databases) will make you much more effective with any of these tools.

Worth noting first: the "most startups fail in year one" idea is a bit of a myth. U.S. data suggests roughly 20% of new businesses close within the first year. Failure rates climb more steeply over five to ten years. Still, early failures tend to share a few causes:

1. **No real demand.** Founders build something they love before confirming that people will pay for it. "Nice idea" isn't the same as "I'll buy that."

2. **Running out of cash.** Everything takes longer and costs more than planned. Without a buffer, a few slow months can be fatal.

3. **Underpricing.** Many founders charge too little to cover costs, hoping volume will save them.

4. **Weak distribution.** A great product nobody hears about still dies. Customer acquisition is often harder than building the product.

5. **Team problems.** Cofounder conflict, missing skills, or burnout can sink things fast.

6. **Lack of focus.** Chasing too many customers, features, or markets at once spreads limited resources thin.

The survivors usually validate early, spend carefully, and adjust quickly.

Congrats on the launch. I've been burned by a couple of no-code tools before, so my first question is always about the exit path. What happens when a customer outgrows you, or you get acquired, or you shut down? Can I export something that runs on its own, like actual code or at least a documented schema plus logic I could rebuild from? Or does the app only exist inside your runtime? Every one of these tools looks great at the demo stage. The pain shows up eighteen months in, when a non-technical founder has built half their business on it and the pricing tier jumps.

The other thing I'd like to see is how you handle the stuff that usually breaks no-code apps at scale: permissions that go beyond "admin vs. user," background jobs, migrating data when the schema changes, and debugging when a workflow silently does the wrong thing. The thing that gets lost in these threads is that 30% made a lot more sense in 2008 than it does now. Back then Apple was handling payment processing, hosting, distribution, and discovery for a store that was genuinely novel, and compared to what carriers were taking for ringtones and J2ME games it looked like a bargain. Fast forward to today: hosting and bandwidth costs have collapsed, payment processing is a commodity at roughly 3%, and discovery is so broken that most devs I know have to buy Apple Search Ads just to show up for their own app name. The rate stayed the same while the value delivered shrank.

The small business program at 15% helped, but it mostly pacified the indie crowd that was making the most noise while leaving the actual structural problem alone. The real issue isn't the percentage, it's that there's no alternative to compare it to. If Apple had to compete with even one credible third-party store or allowed straightforward links to external payment without scare screens, we'd find out pretty quickly what the market thinks distribution on iOS is worth. My guess is it's somewhere well under 30%, and Apple knows it, which is why they've fought every single inch of this in court instead of just letting the market decide.

I've been running a small SaaS on the side for about four years now. It does one boring thing: it generates compliance reports for a niche category of property managers. It brings in a bit over $6k MRR. The thing nobody told me early on is that "profitable" and "sustainable" are different milestones. I hit profitable in month seven because hosting costs were basically nothing. I didn't hit sustainable until I stopped answering support emails at 11pm and put a 24-hour response window in the footer. Not a single customer complained. Most of them were relieved to have a clear expectation.

The biggest lesson was that the market you can reach matters more than the product you can build. I spent my first year adding features nobody asked for, because building was the fun part. Growth only happened once I started showing up in the two forums where my customers actually hang out and answering questions with no link to my product. That built more trust than any landing page tweak. Boring niches are underrated because the competition is usually a spreadsheet, or an enterprise tool that costs 20x more and needs a sales call.

If you're thinking about starting one, my unsolicited advice is to charge more than feels comfortable from day one, and to automate billing and onboarding before anything else. Every manual step you tolerate at 10 customers becomes a second job at 100. And keep your day job longer than your ego wants you to. The side project stayed fun precisely because I never *needed* it to pay rent, and that freedom made me make better decisions.

I think the framing of "the algorithm" as some malevolent puppet master misses what's actually going on. Most of these systems are optimizing for something boring like predicted dwell time or probability of engagement, and they're doing it extremely well. The problem is that what I'll click on at 11pm when I'm tired and irritable is not what I'd choose if you asked me in advance what I want my feed to look like. Recommendation systems are essentially revealed-preference machines, and revealed preferences in a moment of weakness are a terrible proxy for what people actually value. Nobody sat down and decided to make people angrier; the gradient just pointed that way.

What frustrates me is how little control users get over the objective function. Platforms will let you mute a word or click "not interested," but those are tiny nudges against a model trained on billions of interactions that's very confident it knows you better than you do. I'd love a setting that says "optimize for how I feel after closing the app, not how long I stay," even if it's crude. Some of the Bluesky custom feed experiments get close to this idea, and it's telling how much better a dumb chronological or hand-curated feed often feels compared to a sophisticated one.

The counterargument I take seriously is that pure chronological feeds collapse at scale. If you follow more than a few hundred accounts, you get drowned out by whoever posts most, which is its own kind of optimization, just one that rewards volume instead of engagement. So I don't think the answer is "no algorithms," it's algorithms where the ranking criteria are legible and user-adjustable. The technology for that exists; the business incentive mostly doesn't.

I've hit this firsthand. I was writing a fairly mundane sparse matrix routine, and Copilot autocompleted about fifteen lines that looked oddly specific: same variable names, same quirky comment about a "hack for the degenerate case." A quick search turned up the original in a GPL-licensed numerical library, nearly verbatim. Nothing told me where it came from. If I hadn't recognized the style, it would have gone into a proprietary codebase with zero attribution, and nobody would have known until some audit tool flagged it years later.

The "it's just learning patterns, like a human does" argument doesn't hold up when the output is a recognizable chunk of someone else's work. A human who memorized and reproduced fifteen lines of GPL code wouldn't get a pass because they "learned" it. The duplicate-detection filter helps, but it's opt-in on some plans, it misses things that differ by a renamed variable or two, and it puts the burden on the user to have turned it on in the first place. Meanwhile the indemnification promises only cover you if you've configured everything exactly as Microsoft specifies, which tells you how confident they are in the underlying question.

I still use it, because for boilerplate it's genuinely good. But I've started treating any suggestion longer than a few lines that contains "clever" logic as suspect. The tooling should be the one surfacing provenance, not me grepping GitHub after the fact.

My first year I'd ship a feature in the morning and then spend the rest of the day answering emails about why someone's CSV import broke. That said, I wouldn't trade it. Revenue is modest (low six figures, enough to live comfortably in a cheap city), but there's no board, no standups, and if I want to take a Wednesday off to go hiking I just do. If you're thinking about it, pick something boring that businesses already pay for and do it slightly better. The exciting ideas tend to be the ones with ten funded competitors.

I ran a B2B scheduling tool solo for about four years before selling it, and the thing nobody warned me about wasn't the coding or even the marketing. It was the context switching. Monday morning you're debugging a Stripe webhook that silently failed over the weekend, by lunch you're writing a sales email to a prospect who wants SSO, and by evening you're answering a support ticket from someone who can't find the export button that's been in the same place for two years. Each of those is a different brain mode, and there's no one to hand anything off to. The best thing I did was batch ruthlessly: support in two fixed windows a day, no code deploys on Fridays, and sales calls only on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

On the technical side, boring tech won every single time. Postgres, a monolith, server-rendered pages with a sprinkle of JS, one VPS plus managed backups. I watched peers burn months on Kubernetes setups and microservices for products with 40 customers. When you're solo, every piece of infrastructure is something you personally get paged for at 3am, so the bar for adding anything new should be really high. I'd also say charge more than feels comfortable from day one. My churn actually dropped when I raised prices, because the customers paying $15/month were the ones generating 80% of the support load.

The part I'd do differently is building a support network earlier. Being solo doesn't have to mean being isolated. I eventually joined a small group of other indie founders who met on a call every two weeks, and just having people to sanity-check pricing changes or vent to about a nightmare customer made a huge difference to my mental health. The loneliness is real, and it's the thing that actually kills a lot of solo projects, more than any technical or market problem.

The part that always gets me is the timeline. Breach discovered in March, "contained" in April, disclosed in November, and the notification email still leads with "we take your privacy seriously." If you did, you wouldn't have kept SSNs in a plaintext table that a contractor's VPN creds could reach. Every one of these postmortems reads the same: flat network, no segmentation, an internal service with way too much read access that nobody audited because it "just worked."

What I'd actually like to see is the liability math change. Right now the cost of a breach for the company is a year of free credit monitoring (which is worth basically nothing since we've all had our data leaked five times over), a settlement that works out to $4.30 per affected person after lawyers take their cut, and a dip in the stock that recovers by next earnings. Meanwhile the cost of doing it right is real headcount and real friction for product teams. Until those numbers flip, the rational move for a big company is to underinvest in security and budget for the cleanup.

The only things I've seen actually move the needle at places I've worked were data minimization mandates. Not "encrypt everything," which people do badly, but "you are not allowed to store this field at all unless you can justify it to someone who can say no." The data you never collected can't leak. Most of what gets exposed in these breaches is stuff the company had no business keeping past the initial transaction anyway.

I ran into the same failure on my M1 MacBook and found a workaround. The problem seems to be that one of the native dependencies doesn't ship a prebuilt arm64 binary, so the build tries to compile it from source and fails while linking against x86_64 libraries pulled in from an older Homebrew install under /usr/local. You can get around this by running the build under Rosetta. Open a terminal with Rosetta enabled (right-click Terminal in Finder, choose Get Info, check "Open using Rosetta"), or prefix your build command with arch -x86_64. Clear out the existing node_modules folder and any cached build artifacts first so the dependency is fetched again as an x86_64 binary.

If you'd like to stay native on arm64, a cleaner option is to make sure your toolchain is consistent. Install Homebrew under /opt/homebrew (the default location for Apple Silicon), reinstall the affected system libraries there, and confirm that your shell's PATH puts /opt/homebrew/bin ahead of /usr/local/bin. After a clean reinstall of dependencies, the native module should compile correctly against arm64 libraries. This has worked reliably for me, though a proper upstream fix that publishes arm64 prebuilds would make this unnecessary. Happy to help test a PR if anyone picks that up.

Honestly, you won't know from thinking about it. You find out by testing it with real people. A few practical steps:

1. **Name the problem, not the app.** Can you describe the specific pain in one sentence? If not, the idea isn't ready yet.
2. **Look for people already struggling.** Search Reddit, forums, and reviews of competing apps. Complaints and clunky workarounds (spreadsheets, sticky notes, three apps duct-taped together) are great signs.
3. **Competition is usually good.** It proves demand. The question is whether you can do it noticeably better for a specific group.
4. **Talk to 10–15 potential users.** Ask about their current behavior, not whether they'd use your app. People are polite liars about hypotheticals.
5. **Test commitment.** Build a simple landing page and see if anyone signs up, joins a waitlist, or pre-pays. Interest is cheap; action isn't.
6. **Build the smallest possible version.** Ship something rough in weeks, not months.

A good idea is one people actually use, not one that sounds clever.

It depends on your goals, but for most beginners I'd suggest web development first.

**Why web dev first:**
- **Faster feedback.** You build something visible within days, which keeps you motivated.
- **Lower barrier.** You need basic programming, not linear algebra, statistics, and calculus.
- **Practical skills transfer.** Git, APIs, debugging, databases, and deployment all matter in ML work too.
- **Easier job entry.** There are more junior web roles than junior ML roles, which often expect a degree or strong math background.

**When ML first makes sense:**
- You already have a solid math/stats background.
- You're aiming for research, data science, or academia.
- You're genuinely fascinated by data and models. Interest beats strategy.

**A middle path:** Learn Python well. It's used for both (Django/Flask for web; NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn for ML). Build a small web app, then try deploying a simple ML model behind it.

Either way, the most important thing is to pick one, build real projects, and stay consistent.

So there's a bunch of ways actually, and most apps use more than one.

The big one is ads. You see banners or videos, and advertisers pay the app maker per view or click. That's why so many free games spam you with ads between levels lol.

Then there's in-app purchases, like gems, coins, extra lives, skins, whatever. Most people never pay a cent but a small number of people (sometimes called "whales") spend a LOT and basically fund the whole thing.

Freemium is another one, where the basic app is free but you pay for premium features or a subscription. Think Spotify or Duolingo.

Also data. Some apps collect info about how you use them and use it to target ads better or sell insights to other companies. This is the part people don't love.

And sometimes the app isn't really the product, like a bank's app or a store's app, it just gets you to spend money elsewhere.

Anyway yeah, "free" usually means you're paying some other way.

Yeah, you can, depending on what "app" means to you.

If it's something like a booking tool, an internal tracker for your small business, or a simple directory, no-code tools like Bubble, Glide, Softr, or FlutterFlow will get you surprisingly far. I built a little inventory app for my sister's shop in Glide over a weekend and she still uses it. AI coding tools have also gotten good enough that you can describe what you want and get something working.

Where it falls apart is when things get custom or start to scale. Weird integrations, performance problems, or something breaks and you have no idea why. That's when not knowing *anything* about how code works really hurts.

My honest advice is to start no-code and ship something ugly. You'll learn a ton about how apps actually work along the way, and if you outgrow the tool, you'll know exactly what to learn next, or what to hire someone for.
